arXiv:2410.19330v1 [math.PR] 25 Oct 2024

Moments of Gamma type and three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function

Min Wang Address: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Wuhan University, Wuhan 430072, China Email address: minwang@whu.edu.cn
Abstract.

We study a class of positive random variables having moments of Gamma type, whose density can be expressed by the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler functions. We give some necessary conditions and some sufficient conditions for their existence. As a corollary, we give some conditions for non-negativity of the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler functions. As an application, we study the infinite divisibility of the powers of half α\alpha-Cauchy variable. In addition, we find that a random variable 𝐗{\bf X} having moment of Gamma type if and only if log⁡𝐗\log{\bf X} is quasi infinitely divisible. From this perspective, we can solve many Hausdorff moment problems of sequences of factorial ratios.

Key words and phrases: 
Moments of Gamma type; Mittag-Leffler function; alpha-Cauchy distribution; Infinite divisibility; Hausdorff moment problem
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
33E12, 60E10, 60E07, 60E05

1. Introduction

1.1. Moments of Gamma type

Let 𝐗{\bf X} be a positive random variable having moments of Gamma type, namely, for ss in some interval,

Typical examples are the laws of products of independent random variables with Gamma and Beta distribution. For more examples, we refer to Janson [11, Section 3]. Random variables having moments of Gamma type have also been studied in Chamayou and Letac [5], Dufresne [7, 8], Młotkowski and Penson [16], Bosch [3], Karp and Prilepkina [13], Kadankova, Simon and Wang [12], Ferreira and Simon [9], and the references therein. We will review some previous results in Section 2.

1.2. Three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function

From the point of view of special functions, the density of 𝐗a,b,c,d{\bf X}_{a,b,c,d} can be expressed by the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function.

The classical Mittag-Leffler function is the entire function

Eρ​(z):=∑n≥0znΓ⁡(1+ρ​n),z∈ℂ,ρ>0.E_{\rho}(z):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}}{\Gamma(1+\rho n)},\quad z\in\mathbb{C},\,\rho>0.

It was introduced by Gosta Mittag-Leffler in 1903. Wiman introduced the two-parametric Mittag-Leffler function in 1905 and defined it as

Eρ,μ(z):=∑n≥0znΓ⁡(μ+ρ​n),z∈ℂ,ρ,μ>0.E_{\rho,\mu}(z):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}}{\Gamma(\mu+\rho n)},\quad z\in\mathbb{C},\,\rho,\mu>0.

Let ρ>0\rho>0, μ>0\mu>0 and γ>0\gamma>0, the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function is defined as

Eρ,μγ​(z):=∑n≥0Γ⁡(γ+n)Γ⁡(γ)​Γ​(1+n)​Γ​(μ+ρ​n)​zn,z∈ℂ.E_{\rho,\mu}^{\gamma}(z):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{\Gamma(\gamma+n)}{\Gamma(\gamma)\Gamma(1+n)\Gamma(\mu+\rho n)}z^{n},\quad z\in\mathbb{C}.

It can also be represented via the Mellin-Barnes integral:

(1.9) Eρ,μγ​(z)=12​π​i​∫LΓ⁡(s)​Γ​(γ−s)Γ⁡(γ)​Γ​(μ−ρ​s)​(−z)−s​𝑑s,E_{\rho,\mu}^{\gamma}(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{L}\frac{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(\gamma-s)}{\Gamma(\gamma)\Gamma(\mu-\rho s)}(-z)^{-s}ds,

where |arg​z|<π|\text{arg}\,z|<\pi, the contour of integration begins at c−i​∞c-i\infty, ends at c+i​∞c+i\infty, 0<c<γ0<c<\gamma, and separates all poles of the integrand at s=−k,k=0,1,2,⋯s=-k,k=0,1,2,\cdots to the left, and all poles at s=n+γ,n=0,1,⋯s=n+\gamma,n=0,1,\cdots to the right. Applying the Mellin inversion formula to (1.9) we obtain, for 0<s<γ0<s<\gamma,

(1.10) ∫0∞ts−1​Eρ,μγ​(−t)​𝑑t=Γ⁡(s)​Γ​(γ−s)Γ⁡(γ)​Γ​(μ−ρ​s).\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{s-1}E_{\rho,\mu}^{\gamma}(-t)dt=\frac{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(\gamma-s)}{\Gamma(\gamma)\Gamma(\mu-\rho s)}.

Therefore, the density of 𝐗a,b,c,d−1{\bf X}_{a,b,c,d}^{-1} (a,b,c,d>0a,b,c,d>0) is proportional to tb−1​Ed,c+b​da+b​(−t)t^{b-1}E_{d,c+bd}^{a+b}(-t), see (4.3) for details. We then deduce the non-negativity of the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function in some cases.

Recall that a non-negative function ff on (0,∞)(0,\infty) is called completely monotonic if it has derivatives of all orders and (−1)n​f(n)​(x)≥0(-1)^{n}f^{(n)}(x)\geq 0 for n≥1n\geq 1 and x>0x>0. The complete monotonicity of the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function has been well-studied, see e.g. [10, 24], it is proved that if 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1 and 0<γ​ρ≤μ0<\gamma\rho\leq\mu, then Eρ,μγ​(−z)E_{\rho,\mu}^{\gamma}(-z) is completely monotonic. However, we did not find reference on the non-negativity of the three-parametric Mittag-Leffler function.

1.3. Powers of half α\alpha-Cauchy variable

Finally, we investigate the infinite divisibility of the powers of half α\alpha-Cauchy variable. The main tools are Theorem 1.2 and the Kristiansen’s Theorem:

Theorem 1.5 (Kristiansen [14]).

The independent product 𝐖×𝚪2{\bf W}\times{\bf\Gamma}_{2} is ID for any non-negative random variable 𝐖{\bf W}.

As a generalization of the standard Cauchy distribution 1π​11+x2\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}, the α\alpha-Cauchy distribution, denoted by 𝒞α\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}, with density

(1.11) f𝒞α​(t)=sin⁡(π/α)2​π/α​11+|t|α,α>1,t∈ℝ,f_{\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}}(t)=\frac{\sin(\pi/\alpha)}{2\pi/\alpha}\frac{1}{1+|t|^{\alpha}},\quad\alpha>1,\,\,t\in\mathbb{R},

was introduced by Yano, Yano and Yor [26]. They proposed three open questions ([26, Remark 2.9]):

  1. (1)

    Is 𝒞α\mathcal{C}_{\alpha} SD (or ID at least)?

  2. (2)

    Is |𝒞α||\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}| SD (or ID at least)?

  3. (3)

    Is |𝒞α|−p|\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}|^{-p} SD (or ID at least) for p>0p>0?

There are very few results about these questions. Bondesson [1] proved that |𝒞α||\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}| is ID for 1<α≤21<\alpha\leq 2. Diédhiou [6] proved that |𝒞2||\mathcal{C}_{2}| is SD. In the present paper, we establish the infinite divisibility of the powers of |𝒞α||\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}| in many cases, which extend Bondesson’s theorem.

Theorem 1.6.

The random variable |𝒞α|ε​p,ε=±1,|\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}|^{\varepsilon p},\varepsilon=\pm 1, is ID if

(1.12) p≥{(α+1)/3,ε=1, 1<α≤2.α/2,ε=1,α>2.α/2,ε=−1, 1<α≤2.(2​α−1)/3,ε=−1,α>2.p\geq\begin{cases}(\alpha+1)/3,&\quad\varepsilon=1,\,1<\alpha\leq 2.\\ \alpha/2,&\quad\varepsilon=1,\,\alpha>2.\\ \alpha/2,&\quad\varepsilon=-1,\,1<\alpha\leq 2.\\ (2\alpha-1)/3,&\quad\varepsilon=-1,\,\alpha>2.\\ \end{cases}

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review some previous results on the existence of random variables having moments of Gamma type. In section 3, we discuss the connection between moments of Gamma type and Hausdorff moment problem. In Section 4, we prove our results.

2.2. Quasi-infinite divisibility

It is obvious that 𝐗{\bf X} exists if 𝐘:=log⁡𝐗{\bf Y}:=\log{\bf X} is infinitely divisible (ID), we refer to Bondesson [2], Sato [21], Steutel and Van Harn [25] for various accounts on infinite divisibility, self-decomposability (SD), generalized Gamma convolutions (GGC) and hyperbolically completely monotone (HCM) densities. But the reverse direction does not hold, namely

(2.9) 𝐗 exists ⇏ 𝐘 is ID.\text{${\bf X}$ exists $\,\nRightarrow\,$ ${\bf Y}$ is ID}.

For example ([12, Remark (c), page 5]), if 𝐗=D⁡[ab(2​a+b,a+1/2)−]{\bf X}=D\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}a&b\\ (2a+b,a+1/2)&-\end{array}\right], see (2.5) for definition, then 𝐘{\bf Y} is not ID. If 𝐗{\bf X} is the random variable such that J=K=3,Aj=Bk=1,aj=jJ=K=3,\,A_{j}=B_{k}=1,\,a_{j}=j, and bkb_{k} satisfying

1+0.0151+p−0.252+p+13+p=(b1+p)​(b2+p)​(b3+p)(1+p)​(2+p)​(3+p),1+\frac{0.015}{1+p}-\frac{0.25}{2+p}+\frac{1}{3+p}=\frac{(b_{1}+p)(b_{2}+p)(b_{3}+p)}{(1+p)(2+p)(3+p)},

𝐗{\bf X} exists, but 𝐘{\bf Y} is not ID. See [8, Example 2, page 2195] for more details.

The characteristic function of 𝐘{\bf Y} is given by (1.6). The well-known Malmsten formula (see for instance Carmona, Petit and Yor [4]) for the Gamma function is as follows

(2.10) Γ⁡(z+a)Γ⁡(a)=exp⁡{ψ⁡(a)​z+∫0∞(e−z​x−1+z​x)​e−a​x​d​xx⁡(1−e−x)},Re​(z)>−Re​(a),Re​(a)>0.\frac{\Gamma(z+a)}{\Gamma(a)}=\exp\left\{\psi(a)z+\int_{0}^{\infty}(e^{-zx}-1+zx)\frac{e^{-ax}dx}{x(1-e^{-x})}\right\},\,\,\text{Re}(z)>-\text{Re}(a),\,\text{Re}(a)>0.

(2.11) ∑j=1Je−taj/Aj1−e−t/Aj−∑k=1Ke−tbk/Bk1−e−t/Bk≥0,∀t>0.\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{e^{-t\,a_{j}/A_{j}}}{1-e^{-t/A_{j}}}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{e^{-t\,b_{k}/B_{k}}}{1-e^{-t/B_{k}}}\geq 0,\quad\forall\,t>0.

However, the condition (2.11) is not easy to verify. Karp and Prilepkina [13, Theorem 5] have provided some practical sufficient condition. By (2.9), the sufficient condition (2.11) is not necessary. Shanbhag and Sreehari [23, Theorem 2] proved that log⁡𝚪a\log{\bf\Gamma}_{a} is SD for any a>0a>0. If 𝐗{\bf X} exists, then by comparing the Laplace transform we have

Using the terminology in Lindner, Pan and Sato [15], we have the equivalence

However, characterizing the existence of quasi-ID distributions in a given framework is a hard question. It would be interesting to construct more quasi-ID distributions with the help of the Gamma function.

3. Connections to Hausdorff moment problem

In this section, we discuss the connection between moments of Gamma type and Hausdorff moment problem. Roughly speaking, for a given sequence (m0,m1,⋯)(m_{0},m_{1},\cdots), moment problem asks for necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a random variable XX such that 𝔼⁡(Xn)=mn/m0\mathbb{E}(X^{n})=m_{n}/m_{0}, and we call it a moment sequence if such XX exists. There are three well-known moment problems: the Hamburger moment problem deals with all random variables taking values in the whole real line, the Stieltjes moment problem deals with non-negative random variables, and the Hausdorff moment problem deals with random variables on compact real intervals, which is the one we consider here. It is worth mentioning that a Stieltjes or a Hamburger moment problem may have infinitely many solutions if it is solvable (indeterminate moment problem) whereas a Hausdorff moment problem always has a unique solution if it is solvable (determinate moment problem).

The support of 𝐗{\bf X} is [0,D​∏j=0JAjAj​∏k=0KBk−Bk][0,D\prod_{j=0}^{J}A_{j}^{A_{j}}\prod_{k=0}^{K}B_{k}^{-B_{k}}] if Aj>0A_{j}>0 for all jj and γ=0\gamma=0, see (23) of [13]. Recall that γ=∑j=1J|Aj|−∑k=1K|Bk|.\gamma=\sum_{j=1}^{J}|A_{j}|-\sum_{k=1}^{K}|B_{k}|. In this case, the problem of the existence of 𝐗{\bf X} is equivalent to the Hausdorff moment problem of the sequence

(3.1) μn=∏j=1JΓ⁡(Aj​n+aj)∏k=1KΓ⁡(Bk​n+bk),n≥0.\mu_{n}=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{J}\Gamma(A_{j}n+a_{j})}{\prod_{k=1}^{K}\Gamma(B_{k}n+b_{k})},\quad n\geq 0.

We give a family of sequences of factorial ratios which are Hausdorff moment sequences, and then use it to recover some examples in the literature.

Proposition 3.1.

If J=KJ=K, Aj=Bk=1A_{j}=B_{k}=1 for all j,kj,k, 0≤a1≤a2≤⋯, 0≤b1≤b2≤⋯0\leq a_{1}\leq a_{2}\leq\cdots,\;0\leq b_{1}\leq b_{2}\leq\cdots, and ∑j=1Laj≤∑j=1Lbj\sum_{j=1}^{L}a_{j}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{L}b_{j} for each L=1,2,⋯,JL=1,2,\cdots,J, then (μn)n≥0(\mu_{n})_{n\geq 0} defined by (3.1) is a Hausdorff moment sequence.

This proposition is a direct consequence of [13, Theorem 5 (c)], (2.11) and (2.13), we omit the proof. By Proposition 3.1 and the Gauss multiplication formula

Γ(mz)(2π)m−12=mm​z−12Γ(z)Γ(z+1m)⋯Γ(z+m−1m),\Gamma(mz)(2\pi)^{\frac{m-1}{2}}\,=\,m^{mz-\frac{1}{2}}\Gamma(z)\Gamma(z+\frac{1}{m})\cdots\Gamma(z+\frac{m-1}{m}),

we can easily verify that the sequences

μn(1)=Γ⁡(2​n+1)Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(n+1),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(1)}=\frac{\Gamma(2n+1)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(n+1)}, μn(2)=Γ⁡(6​n+1)​Γ​(n+1)Γ⁡(3​n+1)​Γ​(2​n+1)​Γ​(2​n+1),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(2)}=\frac{\Gamma(6n+1)\Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(3n+1)\Gamma(2n+1)\Gamma(2n+1)},
μn(3)=Γ⁡(3​n+1)Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(2​n+1),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(3)}=\frac{\Gamma(3n+1)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(2n+1)}, μn(4)=Γ⁡(3​n+3)Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(2​n+3),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(4)}=\frac{\Gamma(3n+3)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(2n+3)},
μn(5)=Γ⁡(6​n+1)​Γ​(4​n+1)Γ⁡(2​n+1)​Γ​(3​n+1)​Γ​(5​n+1),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(5)}=\frac{\Gamma(6n+1)\Gamma(4n+1)}{\Gamma(2n+1)\Gamma(3n+1)\Gamma(5n+1)}, μn(6)=Γ⁡(5​n+1)Γ⁡(2​n+1)​Γ​(3​n+1),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(6)}=\frac{\Gamma(5n+1)}{\Gamma(2n+1)\Gamma(3n+1)},
μn(7)=Γ⁡(4​n+2)Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(3​n+4),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(7)}=\frac{\Gamma(4n+2)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(3n+4)}, μn(8)=Γ⁡(4​n+4)Γ⁡(n+1)​Γ​(3​n+6),\displaystyle\mu_{n}^{(8)}=\frac{\Gamma(4n+4)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(3n+6)},

are all Hausdorff moment sequence. The sequences μ(1),μ(3),μ(4),μ(6)\mu^{(1)},\mu^{(3)},\mu^{(4)},\mu^{(6)} are binomial sequences, whose moment problem has been totally solved by Młotkowski and Penson [16]. The sequences μ(7),μ(8)\mu^{(7)},\mu^{(8)} are the first two terms of the combinatorial numbers of Brown and Tutte, whose moment problem was investigated by Penson et al. [17]. At the end of [17], the authors said ”we believe that the sequence A⁡(M,n)A(M,n) belongs to a larger family of moment sequences for which analogous relations of type ⋯\cdots”, our Proposition 3.1 gives a kind of such family, but it is not optimal, we leave this question to further research.
